repos.title: Zero-Mem: Zero-Token Memory Operations for LLM Agents
repos.paper_summary: Zero-Mem is a memory system for LLM agents in which no operation outside final question answering calls an LLM or consumes LLM tokens. It keeps the raw interaction traces as the source of record and builds two non-generative views over them: an entity–context co-occurrence graph and a temporal hierarchy of turns, windows, episodes, and local spans. For each query, a deterministic profile sets which view takes priority. The method fuses the two rankings, expands them with graph propagation and neighboring context, and applies deterministic filtering and ranking before one reader LLM answers. On LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini, average F1 is 59.15, versus 53.75 for GAM, the strongest baseline. On HotpotQA at 56K tokens, F1 is 72.07, versus 63.22 for GAM. Memory-operation time drops from 788.76 s for LightMem, the fastest baseline, to 334.77 s, a 57.6% reduction. Limitations: on LoCoMo multi-hop with GPT-4o-mini, F1 is 41.61, below GAM's 42.29; spaCy NER and BGE-M3 embeddings are counted separately from the zero-token claim; and results cover two backbone LLMs and one hardware setup.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agent memory systems often call an LLM for memory operations, and this work asks whether structured access needs generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior systems such as Zep, Mem0, and LightMem reduce memory cost, but many keep generative steps in the memory lifecycle.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Memory is formalized as a function returning evidence from the history, which a reader model then uses to answer.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-Mem selects evidence from raw traces using a graph view, a hierarchy view, routing, closure, and deterministic calibration.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-Mem scores highest on HotpotQA and on LoCoMo averages, while cutting memory-operation time 57.6% versus LightMem.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Structured agent memory can work without generated intermediate representations, with competitive performance and no memory-operation token cost.

repos.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
repos.paper_summary:
Graph RAG is a method for answering global questions over large text corpora by using an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph and pre-generate hierarchical community summaries. The pipeline extracts entities and relationships from source text chunks, partitions the resulting graph into communities using the Leiden algorithm, and summarizes each community. At query time, it generates partial answers from community summaries in parallel and synthesizes them into a final response. This differs from standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which retrieves local text chunks and fails on corpus-wide sensemaking questions.

The authors evaluated Graph RAG against naïve RAG and a map-reduce baseline that summarizes raw source texts directly. They used two datasets of approximately 1 million tokens and 125 LLM-generated sensemaking questions per dataset. An LLM-as-a-judge assessed answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness. Global approaches outperformed naïve RAG, with comprehensiveness win rates between 72% and 83%. Intermediate-level community summaries provided better comprehensiveness and diversity than source-text summarization while using 26–33% fewer context tokens. Root-level summaries reduced token usage by over 97% compared to source-text processing. Limitations include evaluation on only two specific datasets and question types, with no validation of fabrication rates or end-user utility.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RAG cannot answer corpus-wide sensemaking questions, so GraphRAG builds an entity graph with community summaries and outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers graph-based retrieval, hierarchical summaries and benchmarks oriented toward explicit fact retrieval rather than global questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects Leiden communities, summarizes them, and answers queries by map-reduce over summaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare six conditions on two corpora of about one million tokens, using generated global sensemaking questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Global GraphRAG conditions beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness at 72-83% win rates on podcast transcripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation covers only two corpora and lacks a fabrication-rate comparison, which the authors name as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Root-level community summaries give a data index that beats vector RAG and competes with other global methods at lower token cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extraction prompts, self-reflection gleaning, community detection, context window tests, an example comparison, and system prompts.

repos.title: FlashInfer: Efficient and Customizable Attention Engine for LLM Inference Serving
repos.paper_summary: FlashInfer is a customizable attention engine for LLM inference serving that unifies KV-cache storage and supports dynamic scheduling. It uses a block-sparse row format to represent diverse KV-cache layouts, such as paged and radix trees, and employs composable formats to optimize memory access for shared prefixes. A Just-In-Time compiler generates CUDA kernels from user-defined attention variants, while a load-balanced scheduler distributes work across GPU streaming multiprocessors to handle variable sequence lengths. The system maintains compatibility with CUDAGraphs by using persistent kernels and fixed workspace layouts. Experiments on NVIDIA A100 and H100 GPUs show FlashInfer reduces inter-token latency by 29–69% compared to Triton backends in SGLang, cuts long-context inference latency by 28–30% via fused RoPE kernels, and speeds up parallel generation by 13–17%. Limitations include support only for forward-pass attention computation and a roughly 10% performance gap between sparse and dense KV-cache prefill kernels due to restrictions on Tensor Memory Accelerator usage.

repos.title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
repos.paper_summary: uni-robot-agent is a unified, modular harness that lets open-weight models act as robot-use agents in simulation and on physical robots. It gives agents shared tools with common units and feedback across environments through per-environment adapters, overlaps model reasoning with tool execution, and binds images, calibration, and robot state to immutable snapshots. On RoboDojo's 42 simulation tasks (252 episodes), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the harness scores 31.39 with 25.00% success. This is above the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97 and the listed VLA and WAM baselines, and the agent receives no simulator depth or task-verifier feedback. On 19 real-world tabletop tasks it scores 49.50, above Dream-1 (35.50) and close to a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ (47.75). Limitations: real-world agents receive RealSense depth while $\pi_{0.5}$ and Dream-1 use RGB only; precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain weak, and Qwen and DeepSeek trail Xiaomi-Robotics-1 and OpenWAM-$\alpha$ on long-horizon tasks. Trajectory analysis finds four failure patterns, which the authors link to visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Proprietary models block robot-use training, so this paper offers an open, trainable harness that reaches competitive scores.

digest_headlines.heading: uni-robot-agent: A Unified and Modular Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Shared tools, five logical layers, and six design choices let agents run without simulator depth or verifier feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Can Open Models Use Robots in Simulation and the Real World?
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches 31.39 Score on RoboDojo and 49.50 on 19 real-world tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: What Capabilities Enable Robot-Use Agents?
digest_headlines.headline: Robot use appears across model generations and families, and four failure types suggest joint training targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Privileged Information
digest_headlines.headline: Removing camera parameters drops Qwen to 9.13, while removing skills changes Score from 31.39 to 30.31.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis on Cost and Speed
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen costs 1.09 USD per episode for 31.39 Score, and pipelining cuts episode time on all five tested tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior robot-use harnesses offer varied tools and interfaces, so this work separates shared tools from model runtimes.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: An open-weight model with the harness reaches 31.39 Score, while precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain open.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists baselines, real-world task catalogue and scoring rules, per-task results, and agent case studies.

repos.title: Gradio: Hassle-Free Sharing and Testing of ML Models in the Wild
repos.paper_summary:
Gradio is an open-source Python package that generates a web-based interface for machine learning models, allowing non-technical users to test them via a shared URL. The system supports inputs and outputs for images, text, and audio, and is compatible with Scikit-Learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or arbitrary Python functions. When a researcher launches the interface, Gradio creates an SSH tunnel to host the model on the original machine, enabling remote collaborators to access it through a browser without installing software. Users can manipulate inputs, such as cropping or occluding image regions, and flag incorrect predictions to send feedback directly to the developer.

The authors validated the tool in a pilot study involving an ML researcher and a cardiologist classifying echocardiograms for pacemaker presence. The underlying model achieved an AUC of 0.93. Setup took approximately 10 minutes. During testing, the cardiologist successfully identified model failures by flipping images vertically and used the built-in tools to verify predictions by occluding the pacemaker. Limitations include the study's small scope of one user pair over a short period, and the absence of quantitative measures for trust or satisfaction.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Domain experts usually cannot try ML models during development, so the authors built Gradio, a Python package that generates web interfaces.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Interviews with 12 ML researchers yielded four design requirements for interfaces, sharing, input manipulation, and notebook embedding.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: Gradio wraps a trained model in an Interface object with four required parameters and shares it through a secure tunnel.

digest_headlines.heading: Pilot Study: Echocardiogram Classification
digest_headlines.headline: A single pilot pair found the shared link let a cardiologist probe a pacemaker classifier and flag failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion & Next Steps
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the package to widen domain expert access, but a single short pair study cannot establish usefulness.

repos.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
repos.paper_summary: FlexGlue is a neural matcher that takes a set of query keypoints in one image and predicts their subpixel correspondences in the second image, while also predicting whether the pair is covisible so that non-overlapping pairs are rejected. A CNN backbone (frozen ConvNeXt-B with DINOv3 weights) produces a coarse token grid for each image. A 9-layer Transformer with self- and cross-attention updates the tokens, and a per-layer covisibility head can stop inference early on non-overlapping pairs. Each query gets a coarse position from a windowed softmax over cosine similarities, then a learned sub-cell offset. The model is trained on eight datasets with a joint correspondence, matchability, and covisibility loss. The paper reports that FlexGlue performs similarly to LoMa on sparse relative pose, is competitive with RoMav2 at lower cost, and gets the highest HardMatch mAA@10px in the sparse-to-dense setting. It also reports gains on ETH3D and IMC2025 SfM, InLoc, and a new indoor doppelganger benchmark built from LaMAR. Limitations include zero-shot evaluation on indoor disambiguation, since no indoor training data exists, and the paper notes that dense matching lacks robustness on HardMatch.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse matchers are fast but detector-bound, dense matchers are costly, and both miss visual symmetries.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior matchers either inherit keypoint detector limits or add separate post-hoc disambiguation models; FlexGlue handles both in one network.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: FlexGlue aggregates context over dense token grids and reads out subpixel correspondences only at query keypoints, with covisibility heads.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show FlexGlue is competitive with dense matchers on relative pose at lower matching time, and it improves disambiguation, especially indoors.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion claims top accuracy on two multi-view reconstruction benchmarks and on disambiguation and localization benchmarks, at competitive cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists inference cost, keypoint detector results, benchmark curation, training details, matching modes, and limitations such as correlated errors and depth-edge accuracy drops.

repos.title: Isaac Lab: A GPU-Accelerated Simulation Framework for Multi-Modal Robot Learning
repos.paper_summary:
Isaac Lab is an open-source, GPU-accelerated simulation framework for multi-modal robot learning that extends the capabilities of Isaac Gym. Built on NVIDIA Omniverse, it uses OpenUSD for scene authoring, PhysX for high-fidelity physics, and RTX rendering for photorealistic visuals. The framework employs a modular, manager-based API to unify actuator models, multi-frequency sensor simulation, and domain randomization within a single platform. It supports both reinforcement and imitation learning workflows, including data collection pipelines and teleoperation via VR headsets.

The paper presents Isaac Lab as a technical report detailing its architecture and features rather than proposing a new algorithm with specific performance benchmarks. Evidence includes demonstrations of diverse robotic applications such as whole-body control, contact-rich manipulation, and cross-embodiment mobility. The framework utilizes tiled rendering to batch multiple camera outputs into a single GPU framebuffer, enabling large-scale parallel observation generation without costly host-device transfers. A key limitation is that simulation parameters like friction coefficients must still be set via CPU APIs due to current design constraints in the underlying physics engine. Additionally, while the Newton physics engine integration is underway to improve differentiability and physical realism, it currently supports only a subset of environments compared to the existing PhysX backend.

repos.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
repos.paper_summary: This paper defines State Integrity Collapse (SIC), where a model can restate a persistent constraint but stops applying it to later turns, and introduces StateTrack-Bench to measure it. Each dialogue sets one constraint, adds related distractor turns, and tests compliance at depths 3, 5, 7, 10, and 12 across five categories: numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical rules. Seven provider-pinned models produce 875 scored outputs. A GPT-5.4 judge at temperature 0 scores strict joint retention, which requires both the immediate task and the constraint to be satisfied. A forked branch asks each model to restate the constraint, which separates behavioral drift from declarative fade. Strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% (Gemini-3.1-Pro) to 100.0% (DeepSeek-v4-Flash). Integrity failures make up 88.6% of observed failures, or 84.4% without Gemini-3.1-Pro. Limitations: 25 probes per category limits statistical power, the judge is an LLM (human-human kappa 0.82 to 0.87 on 80 outputs), distractors are non-adversarial, each dialogue has one constraint, and the 50-turn results come from a 40-scenario pilot.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Models can restate a constraint yet stop applying it, and the paper measures this gap across dialogue depth.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers instruction following, dialogue state tracking, and long-context position effects, but not whether remembered constraints stay binding.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark and Metrics
digest_headlines.headline: Strict joint retention counts a response only when it meets both the immediate request and the persistent constraint.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Seven provider-pinned model snapshots are tested at fixed prompts and seeds, with a single GPT-5.4 judge.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: DeepSeek-v4-Flash scores 100.0% strict joint retention while Gemini-3.1-Pro falls to 62.4% and loses 10.0 points by turn 12.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Excluding Gemini-3.1-Pro, numerical constraints at depth 50 show 100.0% recall but 79.2% compliance.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Symbolic constraints fail silently, so retrieval alone is insufficient and monitoring should prioritize them.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Persistent-state evaluation is necessary, since State Integrity Collapse remains the dominant failure even without the most brittle model.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits include 25 probes per category, model-based judging, a 30-scenario pilot, cooperative distractors, and one constraint per dialogue.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Scenarios were team-authored with no personal data, and the main risk is misuse as a blanket model safety ranking.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, confidence intervals, temperature and prompt-variant checks, pilots, state anchoring costs, judge audits, and release details.

repos.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Memorilla is a memory system that gives a frozen LLM query-dependent access to a document collection by supplying a fixed number of soft memory tokens in its input embedding space. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder stores each document once, and a trainable module uses query-conditioned slots and Perceiver-style cross-attention over all stored embeddings to produce K=16 tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder. Training runs in three stages (Wikipedia paraphrase reconstruction, ten reading and QA datasets, then the eight evaluation benchmarks) using negative log-likelihood on answer tokens only.

Across eight benchmarks covering personalization, long-document QA and knowledge-intensive QA, the paper reports the best average performance among compared methods, including full context, RAG-50, MemoRAG, Mem0, xRAG and LLMLingua-2. On FactKG, accuracy is 84.33% versus 80.43% for full context, using 108× fewer document tokens. In TextWorld, RL training of the memory module raises success from 18.6% to 24.2% over full-history in-context learning.

Stated limitations: the encoder was not trained for compression, so fine-grained factual details can be lost, and experiments cover only one Qwen encoder-decoder pair and no coding domains.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla gives a frozen LLM 16 query-dependent memory tokens built from a whole document collection instead of retrieved text.

digest_headlines.heading: Memorilla
digest_headlines.headline: Documents are encoded once, and a trainable module maps each query to K=16 soft memory tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla is compared with retrieval, compression and memory baselines on eight benchmarks using a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Quantitative Results
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla has the highest average score and leads on five of eight benchmarks, with a baseline ahead on NarrativeQA, PersonalizationV4 and PubMedQA.

digest_headlines.heading: What Does Memorilla Learn?
digest_headlines.headline: Memorilla's advantage over retrieval-augmented generation (RAG-50) grows with entity count, while retrieval wins on who and which questions in NarrativeQA.

digest_headlines.heading: Continual Learning with Memorilla
digest_headlines.headline: Reinforcement-trained memory on TextWorld raises the average solve rate and cuts rollouts that exhaust the token budget.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The learned memory interface can serve growing histories with a fixed token count, but it can lose fine-grained factual details.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related work, training data and configuration, benchmark details, memory-token ablations and the TextWorld reinforcement-learning setup.

repos.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
repos.paper_summary: AIPOCH Open-Science is an open-source AI research workbench that exports and imports research sessions as portable `.science` packages. The package keeps recorded relations among task context, executed activities, artifact versions, reviews and retained files, and it maps identifiers to the receiving workspace. The authors specify this exchange contract and test it on one controlled session with an incorrect first output, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted permutation test. Complete and partial exports were compared with source snapshots extracted independently of the exporter, and both imports into separate projects retained the tested version and review associations. The unreviewed revision stayed distinct from earlier assessments, and excluded content was marked unavailable. A separate registry case linked a table to its recorded task, execution and review. Offline re-execution of its retained script on a fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. Limitations stated by the paper include that the controlled test used one session and one installation, that native input-edge rows were absent, and that initial task attribution still depends on the surrounding conversation.

digest_headlines.heading: Author affiliations
digest_headlines.headline: The author list spans many hospitals and companies, mainly in China, with affiliations also in the Netherlands, Israel and the United States.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sharing AI-assisted research needs its task, version and review relations to survive transfer, not only the output files.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier provenance and session-sharing systems cover parts of the problem; this work focuses on version and review attribution after exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods and implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The method maps workbench records into typed objects and relations, then checks an exported package against an independently extracted source reference.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Relations, not just files, survived export in a controlled session, with all paired comparisons matching in both exchange conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A failed assessment, its correction and an unreviewed revision can all be true together, so exchange must keep each target separate.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The contract keeps recorded version and review relations across identifier mapping and explicit omissions, with evidence limited to the tested records.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The software is released under Apache 2.0, and a de-identified validation release on Hugging Face contains the protocol, packages and audit scripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of AI assistance
digest_headlines.headline: Codex assisted with literature retrieval, source inspection, application operation and validation code, and the authors remain responsible for interpretation.

digest_headlines.heading: Supplementary Information
digest_headlines.headline: The supplementary figure lists case16 evidence associations and an offline re-execution that reproduced two saved tables byte for byte.
